Hair controversy

By: Phakamile Hlubi | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Allegations of racism sparked by a school's policy to ban the afro.

Unique Selling Point:
A scandal has erupted at Pretoria Girls High where educators have been accused of racism, because the schools dress code policy allegedly bans Afro's or natural African hair. According to Al Jazeera pupils at the school staged a demonstration after one of the learner's there was disciplined because of an essay that she wrote where she exposed the suffering of black women at the hands of 'white privilege'.

Summary:
The education MEC Panyaza Lesufi visited the school earlier in the week. Pupils at the school gave detailed accounts to official of racism and bullying. They also claimed that the school wouldnt allow them to speak African languages and banned the pupils from speaking in any language other than English.
Pupils gave detailed accounts of racism, they also claimed the teachers wouldn't allow them to speak African languages at the school. Meanwhile at a meeting with teachers and parents it was agreed that the allegations pf racism would be investigated.
In a similar case, Durban Girls High was slammed by the Equality Court in 2005 for preventing a learner from wearing a nose stud, in line with Hindu culture.
We interview a learner from Pretoria Girls High school, Zulaika Patel (or her parents) to get the details of the situation at the school. We also get a response from Pretoria Girls High. We also sit down with MEC Panyaza Lesufi on the situation at PTA girls high and other schools. How does the DBE plan to deal with these issues?
We also chat to Milisuthando Bongela, a blogger and writer who has been outspoken on this issue. She says the problem is that institutions like schools and universities have not changed to reflect the changes in SA society or the constitution. It's not about hair. Its a culture of exclusion which is expressed in the school's code of conduct. Its usually at odds with the constitution.
Terry Oakley Smith an expert in workplace diverty believes that there has not been an honest discussion about race and racism in SA. Smith beleives part of the solution is that educators must be taught to understand cultural differences and nuances. 'To do this they must confront their own bigotry so that they can see the irrationality of their prejudice'.

Press Release:


Students Protest Hair Rules
Teachers at a Pretoria high school have been accused of racism for allegedly forcing black girls to follow strict hairstyle rules. In protest, students have taken a stand against the rules they deem discriminatory by wearing black headwraps and clothing. At a second silent protest on school grounds at the weekend, students were threatened with arrest. This week classes resumed to normal while meetings were held with MEC Panyaza Lesufi to find a way forward. Carte Blanche explores a debate many are saying is about much more than hair and rather about dignity, identity and respect.


Script:


Why is it that when you type in ‘unprofessional hairstyles’ on Google, you get images of mostly black women with Afros?

Many African women find that their natural hair is offensive to some cultures. This past week this issue stirred up allegations of racism and bullying at some of the country’s top schools.

WENDY MAHLOBO, PUPIL, PRETORIA HIGH SCHOOL FOR GIRLS: It breaks you down as a person because you look at yourself and you think, am I good enough for them?

BONGANI LINK: Prosit Spes Labori - We work in hope. It really doesn’t get more traditional than the Pretoria High School for Girls. For generations, institutions like this have been built on a value systems that they believe have stood the test of time.

JOANNE MAHLOBO, PUPIL, PRETORIA HIGH SCHOOL FOR GIRLS: My hair is not an animal. When you say tame your hair, I totally take it as disrespectful and a very racist opinion because you wouldn’t say that to a white girl.

BONGANI LINK: The politics of black hair are complex and multi-layered. Braids, weaves, dreadlocks, relaxers - they often are at the very core of what it means to be black. But what adds a particular sting to this issue is that it’s outsiders who are setting the rules.

Learners at the Pretoria High School for Girls claim the dress code and hair policy has been used for years by some teachers to bully and police black learners.

WENDY MAHLOBO, PUPIL, PRETORIA HIGH SCHOOL FOR GIRLS: We are in a school that promotes equality. So why aren’t we all treated equally? Why does my hair have to be a certain way? Why do I have to be that way? It was basically the school trying to adjust us to be more like them.

Teresa Oakley-Smith, a specialist in diversity management, believes that the process of formulating a dress code policy should be an inclusive one.

TERESA OAKLEY-SMITH, CHANGE MANAGEMENT CONSULTANT: Unless rules and policies are developed with the total environment of people who are going to have to A, apply them, and B, live by them, then whose rules are they?

Black pupils have also accused some of the teachers of calling them monkeys and banning them from speaking their mother tongue at school.

WENDY MAHLOBO, PUPIL, PRETORIA HIGH SCHOOL FOR GIRLS: Since they don’t understand our home languages, they decided to say our home languages terrify them. Those click sounds are terrifying. They don’t understand them.

TERESA OAKLEY-SMITH, CHANGE MANAGEMENT CONSULTANT: That language is somehow inferior because it’s got clicks. And noises that I don’t understand. So it goes back into that perspective of white is right, English or Afrikaans is good, but Zulu, Xhosa whatever, is bad.

Last month one of the educators at the school allegedly victimised a 13-year-old pupil, by disciplining her for writing an essay about how society is still structured to benefit white people.

Fed up with the treatment they said they were receiving, learners staged a silent protest at the school’s Spring Festival last week.

But the protesting learners were confronted by armed security guards, dogs and threats of arrest.

MILISUTHANDO BONGELA, ARTS AND CULTURE EDITOR, MAIL & GUARDIAN: Why should it be okay that dogs are set on children?

Milisuthando Bongela, arts and culture editor of the Mail & Guardian, says this is reminiscent of the Soweto Uprising of 1976.

MILISUTHANDO BONGELA, ARTS AND CULTURE EDITOR, MAIL & GUARDIAN: I mean, that’s bizarre, and we don’t think about that because it’s so normal to see a black body, a black man a black child, in a state of entropy, in a state of poverty, in a state of disdain and pain… it’s so normal. You would never think… It would never happen anywhere in the world, it would never happen!

BONGANI: What about the criticism that some have levelled at the parents of these children who go to schools like the ones that have now come up in the media. Where are the parents?

MILISUTHANDO BONGELA, ARTS AND CULTURE EDITOR, MAIL & GUARDIAN: The parents are also victims of a society that has not prioritised racism as something to truly understand. It’s not about an individual school, it’s not about an individual person, it’s about how we all uphold in some way, we are all in some ways complicit to upholding particular standards that we’ve been taught. Why? Because we are all in a pressure cooker that’s made of racist juice.

The dress code policies at all Gauteng schools will now be reviewed after the education MEC and officials visited the high school and met with pupils, parents and teachers.

Education department spokesperson Oupa Bodibe confirmed that an investigation has been launched into the allegations of racism and a report is expected later this month.

OUPA BODIBE, SPOKESPERSON, GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT: We are very disturbed. Our concern is to make sure that we deal with racism from any quarter and that attitudes need to change. But more importantly, this is not about discipline. Discipline is important, but how you enforce discipline as an adult ... you ought to be sensitive, you are dealing with fragile souls.

BONGANI LINK: Whilst the Pretoria High School for Girls remains the focal point of this controversy, perhaps it has sparked a debate and a discussion that is long overdue for the country as a whole.

TERESA OAKLEY-SMITH, CHANGE MANAGEMENT CONSULTANT: We are not accommodating. We are keeping to the rules of a tiny minority and making it difficult for people that we think of as the other to be part of our communities.

The battle at the Pretoria High School for Girls is a microcosm of a larger issue facing our young democracy. The young women at the forefront of this new struggle are determined not to give up.

OUPA BODIBE, SPOKESPERSON, GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT: The girls will not let us forget, because what I’ve perceived there is that the level of organisation is astounding. The networking and so forth so they will keep pressure and they should.

WENDY MAHLOBO, PUPIL, PRETORIA HIGH SCHOOL FOR GIRLS: I’m not only fighting for myself, I’m fighting for other people who go through this on a daily... Just because you don’t go through it, doesn’t mean there aren’t people who hurt on the other side...

BONGANI LINK: What happens if we don’t get it right?

MILISUTHANDO BONGELA, ARTS AND CULTURE EDITOR, MAIL & GUARDIAN: For now we live at a time where violence is not an option so they do protests. But how does the state respond? With violence. They bring dogs, they bring armed policemen to talk to 13-year-old girls. So they expect the violence. I feel like in South Africa if we do not deal with these things…. the guns are going to come out. The guns are going to come out and people are going to say, but what did you guys expect?

PROMOS

15 SECS:

VO: Could a fight about black hair be breaking open a debate about racism that South Africans can no longer avoid?

MILISUTHANDO BONGELA: It’s not about an individual school, it’s not about an individual person, it’s about how we all uphold in some way, we are all in some ways complicit to upholding particular standards that we’ve been taught.

15 SECS:

VO: Some may think it’s only about hair but the debate raging around the rules enforced on black girls at some schools is about far more than that.

JOANNE MAHLOBO, PUPIL, PRETORIA HIGH SCHOOL FOR GIRLS: My hair is not an animal. When you say tame your hair, I totally take it as disrespectful and a very racist opinion because you wouldn’t say that to a white girl.

10 SECS:
Can the fight over the hair of black schoolgirls be likened to the Soweto Uprisings of 1976?
